title: Northwind x Redwood - POC check-in (perf results + tail latency)
summary: POC weekly check-in focused on reviewing the benchmark spreadsheet (A100/H100/L40S runs) and explaining the p99 behavior for long-context summarization workloads. Redwood walked through how runtime 1.21 kernel auto-selection v2 behaves across seq-length buckets and why one L40S result set showed a tail spike likely due to a mis-bucket / fallback kernel on long prefill. Customer asked about determinism, how to reproduce selection decisions, and what knobs exist to pin/override kernels during rollout. Team aligned on running a dedicated pool test on an H100-only pool first (then mixed A100), using Northwind’s actual prompt distribution and a fixed concurrency target, with Redwood providing the exact runtime flags/telemetry queries and an allowlist config to keep v2 controlled.
topics: Benchmark spreadsheet review: p50/p95/p99 latency deltas vs baseline
Long-context prefill vs decode behavior and seq-length bucketing
GPU SKU differences (H100 vs A100 80GB vs L40S) and stability
Kernel auto-selection v2 determinism, telemetry, and sampling overhead
Plan for a Dedicated pool test and rollout guardrails / rollback
questions: For long-context (16k–32k) prompts, what specific kernel is being selected and can we force it for an A/B run?
If we move to Dedicated, can we request an H100-only pool and avoid mixed SKUs during the POC?
How do we know selection decisions are deterministic across restarts / across hosts?
What are the rollback triggers you recommend (p99 delta threshold, error rate)?
Can Redwood share the exact dashboard queries / fields to break down p99 by seq bucket and GPU SKU?
next_steps: Redwood to send a sanitized export of the benchmark table with notes on the L40S anomaly and the long-context bucket definitions.
Northwind to provide a 24h histogram of prompt lengths (prefill tokens) and target concurrency / throughput goal for the dedicated test.
Redwood to set up a Dedicated trial plan for an H100-only pool and propose a 2-hour canary window to run the same scenario suite.
Redwood to share runtime flags for selection tracing + a minimal telemetry sampling config suitable for POC.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up after the dedicated run to review p99 and decide on next model/GPU configuration.
action_items: Markus Klein (Redwood) - Email dedicated pool options + proposed H100 SKU(s) and region choices - Due 2026-02-20
Isabella Rossi (Redwood) - Add annotation in the spreadsheet for the L40S long-prefill run (suspected fallback kernel) + rerun microbench if needed - Due 2026-02-21
Omar El-Sayed (Redwood) - Send telemetry field list + dashboard links/queries for kernel selection breakdown (model/GPU/seq bucket) - Due 2026-02-20
Priya Shah (Northwind) - Share prompt-length distribution + current p99 SLO target and acceptable regression budget - Due 2026-02-20
Nina Patel (Northwind) - Confirm whether any driver/CUDA constraints exist in their environment for Private later (even if Dedicated first) - Due 2026-02-24
transcript:
Meeting: Northwind x Redwood - POC check-in (perf results + tail latency)
Recorded: 2026-02-19 16:00 PST
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees:
- Markus Klein (Redwood)
- Omar El-Sayed (Redwood)
- Isabella Rossi (Redwood)
- Lauren Bishop (Redwood)
- Priya Shah (Northwind)
- David Lin (Northwind)
- Nina Patel (Northwind)
- Tom Becker (Northwind)

Auto-generated notes (may be inaccurate)
Summary: Reviewed benchmark spreadsheet and tail latency concerns. Aligned on dedicated pool test plan (H100 first) with controlled rollout of kernel selection v2.

Transcript

[00:00] Markus (Redwood): Hey everyone. Can you all hear me okay?
[00:03] Priya (Northwind): Yep, good.
[00:04] Omar (Redwood): Yeah, loud and clear.
[00:06] Tom (Northwind): Yep.
[00:07] Markus (Redwood): Cool. So today we said we’d spend most of the time on the perf sheet you all were updating and specifically the p99 questions on long-context summarization. Isabella’s here because she was looking at the SKU-specific stuff, and Omar can talk telemetry and the tail.
[00:22] Priya (Northwind): Great. We have the spreadsheet open. The tab “v1 vs v2 - Feb 18” is the one.

[00:30] Isabella (Redwood): Yep, I’m on that tab. I might reference row numbers but… I know they move.
[00:35] David (Northwind): No worries.

[00:38] Markus (Redwood): Priya, do you want to recap what you’re seeing that’s worrying you?
[00:43] Priya (Northwind): Sure. So overall the median is fine, p50 is like better in most cases. But the p99 on the 16k to 32k bucket, on L40S specifically, jumped. It’s like, I wrote down, baseline p99 was ~2.1 seconds and then v2 run is like 2.9, 3.0 seconds. It’s enough that it would blow our internal SLO if that’s real.
[01:05] Nina (Northwind): And just to add, it’s not every run. It was like one of the canary runs. But it’s scary because in production you don’t get to pick when you hit the p99.

[01:16] Omar (Redwood): Yep. That’s the right instinct. Tail is where surprises hide.
[01:19] Isabella (Redwood): Also just to sanity check, that’s the “long prefill, short decode” scenario right? The summarization prompts that are huge inputs but then you only generate like, what, 200 tokens.
[01:28] David (Northwind): Exactly. We pass a big document, ask for structured summary, output is short.

[01:34] Omar (Redwood): Okay. So the important nuance: that workload is dominated by prefill, not decode. A lot of people mentally map “LLM latency” to decode tokens/sec, but here it’s prefill time. Kernel selection v2 explicitly buckets based on a prefill/decode regime signal. If that signal mis-classifies a request—like it thinks it’s a balanced decode workload—it can pick a kernel that’s great for steady decode but not great for huge prefill.
[01:58] Priya (Northwind): That’s basically what we’re worried about. So is this misclassification, or is it just L40S being like… weaker?

[02:06] Isabella (Redwood): I think it’s a combo. L40S is a different memory and different “best” kernel in the long prefill. But in the run you’re pointing at, the candidate set for L40S had one kernel denylists in our internal notes for a specific driver. I’m not 100% sure what driver you were on.
[02:22] Nina (Northwind): We used the default in your image. I think it was CUDA 12.2? Driver… I can pull it.
[02:28] Markus (Redwood): That’d help. We also can send you the “print runtime env” command so it’s in the logs.

[02:35] Priya (Northwind): But even if it’s driver, our reality is we might land on those drivers in Dedicated too, unless we control it.
[02:42] Lauren (Redwood): In Dedicated we can control the driver stack per pool, yes. That’s one of the benefits. We can say “H100 pool with driver X” and keep it pinned during POC.
[02:52] Tom (Northwind): That’s helpful.

[02:55] Omar (Redwood): Let me propose how to interpret the sheet. If you look at H100 numbers: p95 and p99 improved or stayed flat across most buckets. A100 also mostly improved. The L40S has the outlier in long prefill. That pattern suggests it’s not “v2 is generally unstable”, it’s “on that SKU and regime, one selection path is suboptimal”. Which is fixable with allow/deny rules, and also by making the long-prefill threshold more conservative.

[03:20] Priya (Northwind): So for our POC, can we just… avoid L40S? Because we don’t need it. We’d rather spend money on fewer, faster GPUs and have stable tail.
[03:28] Markus (Redwood): Yes, that’s exactly what we were going to suggest. Start with H100-only dedicated pool, run your scenario suite, validate p99. Then optionally test A100 80GB if cost matters. L40S is more “cost optimized” but it’s not necessary for your first pass.
[03:44] David (Northwind): We put L40S in because we saw it in some public benchmarks and it’s available in our cloud account, but we can drop it.

[03:53] Isabella (Redwood): And to be clear, we don’t have a philosophical issue with L40S, it’s just more sensitive to kernel choice in the long-prefill case.

[04:01] Nina (Northwind): Okay, but long term, if we did end up with mixed fleets, how does v2 handle heterogenous? Like will it pick different kernels for different SKUs consistently?
[04:10] Omar (Redwood): Yes. v2 keys on GPU SKU, model family, and seq bucket. That’s the “three-axis” thing. So the decision is not “one kernel for all”. It’s “for this model family, on this GPU type, in this regime, pick kernel K”. And we emit telemetry so you can actually see the distribution.

[04:29] Priya (Northwind): We saw in the notes from last time something about determinism. Can you clarify that? We had a bad experience elsewhere where the “auto tuning” changed its mind.
[04:38] Omar (Redwood): Totally. We’re not doing online learned tuning in the hot path. It’s rule-based plus a registry. So given the same inputs—model hash/version, GPU SKU normalized, and the extracted seq regime—you get the same decision. There’s no randomness. The only way it changes is if you change the config or the registry version, or you roll out a new runtime.
[04:59] David (Northwind): What about, like, if the scheduler passes in “observed distribution hints” and that changes over time? Does that change selection?
[05:07] Omar (Redwood): Good catch. There is an optional hint channel. In Dedicated we can either turn it off or keep it read-only for stability. And even if it’s on, it’s still deterministic per window, but the window could drift if your traffic mix changes. For your POC we can lock it down: use request-local features only, no adaptive hints.
[05:27] Priya (Northwind): That sounds good. Lock it down please.

[05:30] Markus (Redwood): Isabella, can you walk through what you think happened in that L40S spike? Like, plain English.
[05:36] Isabella (Redwood): Yeah. So the long-context run: you have big input, short output. v2 tries to detect that and chooses a “prefill-optimized” kernel. On H100/A100 it does. On L40S, the registry has a fallback order. One of the candidates is “fast in median” but has a tail risk when prefill is huge and the workspace gets tight. If it falls back to that kernel—either because the preferred kernel is missing for that driver or it’s marked unstable—then you see occasional long outliers.
[06:06] Nina (Northwind): Workspace gets tight meaning memory?
[06:09] Isabella (Redwood): Yeah, like scratch memory and sometimes you get fragmentation. I’m simplifying, but yes.

[06:15] Priya (Northwind): So if we do H100-only, we basically bypass this whole path.
[06:20] Isabella (Redwood): Pretty much.

[06:23] Tom (Northwind): Okay. But how do we trust that H100 won’t have some other weird corner? We don’t have a huge test budget.
[06:32] Omar (Redwood): We can define clear canary criteria. For example: run 30 minutes of your workload replay on the dedicated pool with v2 on, compare against v1 pinned kernel selection or v1 selector. We set thresholds: p99 must be within, say, +3% of baseline or better; error rate must not increase; and the selection distribution should be stable. If any threshold trips, we flip the gate.
[06:57] Priya (Northwind): When you say “flip the gate”, you mean we can disable v2 without redeploying?
[07:02] Lauren (Redwood): Yes. In Dedicated, it’s a config toggle per model / per pool. It’s basically hot reload.
[07:08] Nina (Northwind): That’s good.

[07:10] David (Northwind): Can we also force a kernel just for the experiment? Like A/B exact same kernel and see if it’s selection overhead.
[07:18] Isabella (Redwood): Yes. There’s a CLI flag that forces kernel choice and can dump the selection trace. I’ll send you the exact flag name after this. It’s something like `--force_kernel=` and `--dump_selector_trace`.
[07:31] Omar (Redwood): And selection overhead is tiny, like microseconds to low milliseconds depending on sampling. The bigger overhead is telemetry if you log every request. So we sample. For POC we can do 0.1% sampling but always sample “slow requests” above a threshold.
[07:49] Priya (Northwind): Always sample slow ones would be ideal.

[07:52] Markus (Redwood): Let’s talk dedicated plan. Lauren, can you outline what we can offer in terms of GPUs and regions for the next week?
[08:00] Lauren (Redwood): Yeah. In us-west we can do an 8xH100 pool pretty quickly, or a 4xH100 if you want smaller. Alternatively A100 80GB is more plentiful. My recommendation: 4xH100 first for the test, because your traffic in POC is not huge. Then if you want to scale and see throughput stability, we can expand to 8x.
[08:22] Tom (Northwind): We’d rather do 4 first.
[08:25] Priya (Northwind): Agreed.

[08:27] Nina (Northwind): Any chance of H100 PCIe vs SXM differences? We’ve seen those show up.
[08:33] Isabella (Redwood): Good question. Yes, there are differences. In our registry we normalize SKU. But the dedicated offering is typically H100 SXM for the 8x nodes. For 4x, it can vary. Lauren, what’s available?
[08:47] Lauren (Redwood): For the trial we can do SXM in an 8x chassis but allocate you 4 GPUs worth of capacity, or we do a smaller PCIe node. It depends on the timing. I’ll confirm and email.
[09:00] Priya (Northwind): Please confirm. We’d prefer consistency over absolute cheapest.

[09:07] Markus (Redwood): Okay. Now, spreadsheet. David, you ran the mixed workload too, right? The one with 70% short prompts, 30% long docs.
[09:16] David (Northwind): Yeah. That one looked fine. p99 didn’t move much. That’s why we were confused why the long-only scenario spiked.
[09:25] Omar (Redwood): That actually fits. In mixed workloads, the scheduler batching can smooth some of the tail. But in long-only, every request is heavy prefill and you can’t “hide” the worst case behind cheap ones.
[09:39] Nina (Northwind): Also in mixed you might have fewer concurrent long ones, depending on arrival.
[09:44] Omar (Redwood): Exactly.

[09:46] Priya (Northwind): For our production, it’s mostly long-only during certain hours. It’s batch summarization.
[09:52] Markus (Redwood): That’s important. So our POC should mirror that: sustained long-only, steady concurrency.

[10:00] Tom (Northwind): What concurrency are you thinking?
[10:03] Priya (Northwind): Our job runner typically does 32 concurrent docs per worker cluster. But we can scale.
[10:10] Omar (Redwood): Let’s pick a target throughput. For example “X docs/minute at p99 < Y seconds”. If you tell us your SLO and volume, we can propose concurrency.
[10:22] Priya (Northwind): Our internal SLO is p99 under 2.4 seconds for the 16k-32k bucket. Volume is like 200k docs/day but it’s spiky.
[10:34] Markus (Redwood): Got it.

[10:36] David (Northwind): Also, we’re doing structured output. Does that change kernel selection? It shouldn’t, but just asking.
[10:43] Isabella (Redwood): It shouldn’t affect kernel selection, no. That’s more on decoding constraints and logit processing, but kernel selection is at attention / matmul level and depends on shapes.

[10:56] Priya (Northwind): So what do we need to provide you before you can set up the dedicated test?
[11:01] Lauren (Redwood): Two things: region preference, and whether you need any special networking like VPC peering for the POC. If it’s just hitting the dedicated endpoint over TLS, we can start without private networking.
[11:13] Nina (Northwind): For the POC, public endpoint is fine. For prod we’ll want VPC, but not for this.
[11:19] Lauren (Redwood): Great, that speeds it up.

[11:22] Omar (Redwood): And from the perf side, we need the prompt length distribution and the exact “max output tokens” you set. Because that affects the prefill/decode regime signal.
[11:33] David (Northwind): We can share a histogram. We have it in Datadog. I can export.
[11:38] Priya (Northwind): I’ll send it.

[11:41] Markus (Redwood): Let’s do the tail latency mechanics question: How do we verify the kernel selection per request? Omar?
[11:48] Omar (Redwood): There are two methods. One is telemetry: we emit a “kernel_selection” event with fields like selected kernel id, gpu sku, model family tag, seq bucket, and whether it was fallback. That can be sampled. Two is local reproduction: enable trace dump on a specific request id. In Dedicated we can set “always dump on slow request” threshold, like >p95.
[12:15] Nina (Northwind): Is that trace dump PII-safe?
[12:18] Omar (Redwood): We don’t dump token content by default. It’s shapes and ids. But we can confirm the fields. You can also keep it internal to your account.

[12:29] Priya (Northwind): In the spreadsheet, can we add a column “chosen kernel” for each run?
[12:33] Isabella (Redwood): Yes, that’s actually a great idea. For the rerun, we can export the distribution: like 80% kernel A, 20% fallback kernel B. That might explain p99.

[12:46] Markus (Redwood): Okay. Quick competitor question that came up internally: you mentioned you tried Bedrock and Together. Anything relevant you want to share? It helps us tailor.
[12:56] Priya (Northwind): Bedrock was easy but we couldn’t get consistent tail on long inputs, and also the model choice was limited. Together was faster on average but we had occasional “mystery slow” and it was hard to debug. That’s why we like the idea of you showing us the kernel selection and stuff.
[13:14] Omar (Redwood): Makes sense.

[13:16] Tom (Northwind): Our leadership is basically asking “can we predict cost and SLO reliably”. Tail is the trust thing.
[13:23] Markus (Redwood): Understood.

[13:25] Nina (Northwind): So dedicated test. Will we be on runtime 1.21?
[13:29] Lauren (Redwood): Yes. Dedicated trial would be on 1.21 with v2 available, but we can start with v1 default and then do a controlled switch.
[13:39] Priya (Northwind): We’d like to start with v1 pinned, then turn v2 on as A/B.
[13:44] Isabella (Redwood): Perfect. We can do that.

[13:48] Omar (Redwood): And we can keep an allowlist: only your model gets v2, and only on H100, and only for your account.
[13:56] David (Northwind): Nice.

[14:00] Markus (Redwood): Let’s revisit the actual numbers. Isabella, can you call out the H100 p99 delta in long prefill scenario?
[14:07] Isabella (Redwood): In your sheet, H100 long prefill: p99 went from ~1.65s to ~1.52s, so about 8% improvement. Throughput was also a bit more stable. A100 was more modest, like 3-5%. L40S had the regression you mentioned.
[14:27] Priya (Northwind): That’s encouraging.

[14:29] Nina (Northwind): And any correctness differences? Like output changes?
[14:34] Markus (Redwood): Kernel selection should not change outputs. It’s deterministic math, same precision mode. We also run conformance tests. But we can include a quick output diff check in the POC harness.
[14:47] David (Northwind): We did spot check. Seems identical.

[14:52] Omar (Redwood): One caveat: if you’re using non-deterministic CUDA settings, you can see tiny floating point differences. But our runtime pins determinism settings in production mode.
[15:03] Priya (Northwind): Okay.

[15:05] Tom (Northwind): What’s your recommended rollback trigger during our POC? Just p99 or also error rate?
[15:12] Omar (Redwood): Both. Specifically: (1) p99 regression above 5% for 10 minutes in the long-context bucket, (2) error rate increase above baseline +0.2% absolute, (3) any spike in timeouts. And we also look at selection distribution: if fallback rate jumps, that’s an early warning.
[15:36] Nina (Northwind): Can we get those as alerts?
[15:39] Omar (Redwood): Yes, we can configure a dashboard and alerting. For POC we might do manual monitoring plus a simple alert.

[15:49] Priya (Northwind): Sampling: we don’t want to pay a ton of overhead. What sampling rate did you say?
[15:55] Omar (Redwood): 0.1% is typical. But for a POC, we can do 1% for a short run. The overhead is mostly log volume. The actual selector is not the cost.
[16:08] David (Northwind): If we do 1% for 2 hours that’s fine.

[16:12] Markus (Redwood): Sounds like we’re converging. Any other open concerns?
[16:17] Priya (Northwind): The only other thing: GPU naming. In the sheet we wrote “A100” but there are like, 40GB, 80GB, MIG, etc. We want to be sure we’re comparing apples to apples.
[16:30] Isabella (Redwood): Yeah. We’ve had confusion there too. In telemetry we normalize the SKU string and include memory size and whether MIG is enabled. For Dedicated we will avoid MIG for this test.
[16:43] Nina (Northwind): Please avoid MIG.
[16:45] Lauren (Redwood): Yep.

[16:47] Tom (Northwind): Timeline: can we do the dedicated test next week?
[16:52] Lauren (Redwood): I believe so. If we can get approval today, we can aim for Tuesday or Wednesday. Markus and I will follow up with exact times.
[17:02] Priya (Northwind): Tuesday works.

[17:05] Omar (Redwood): For the long-context anomaly, we’re also going to rerun that L40S scenario internally with a stricter long-prefill threshold, just to confirm it goes away. But again, you don’t need L40S for the decision.
[17:21] Priya (Northwind): Appreciate it.

[17:23] (crosstalk)
[17:24] Speaker 1: Sorry, one sec—
[17:25] Nina (Northwind): Go ahead, David.
[17:27] David (Northwind): Just wondering: do you cache the kernel selection per model and bucket? Like to avoid recomputing per request.
[17:35] Isabella (Redwood): Yes, there’s a cache keyed on (model, gpu sku, seq bucket, a couple flags). So after warmup it’s basically a lookup.
[17:45] David (Northwind): Great.

[17:47] Markus (Redwood): Okay, let’s outline the concrete plan.
[17:50] Markus (Redwood): Step 1: Northwind sends us prompt length histogram, max output tokens, and target p99 SLO. Step 2: Redwood provisions 4xH100 Dedicated in us-west, confirm SXM vs PCIe. Step 3: We run baseline with v1 pinned selection for 30 minutes. Step 4: Enable v2 gate for your model only, run same load. Step 5: Compare p95/p99 and selection distribution; decide go/no-go.

[18:18] Priya (Northwind): That’s good.
[18:20] Nina (Northwind): What tool do you want us to use to generate load? We have Locust.
[18:25] Omar (Redwood): Locust is fine. We can also provide a simple Python harness. But use what you already trust.
[18:33] Priya (Northwind): We’ll use our harness.

[18:36] Lauren (Redwood): On networking, since it’s public endpoint for now, you can start as soon as the pool is up.
[18:42] Tom (Northwind): Great.

[18:44] Omar (Redwood): I’ll send you the telemetry fields and a couple queries: break down p99 by seq bucket, and show fallback rate by GPU. Also a “top kernels by count” view.
[18:58] Priya (Northwind): Perfect.

[19:01] Markus (Redwood): Any procurement blockers for the dedicated trial?
[19:05] Tom (Northwind): Not yet. We’re still in evaluation. If this looks good, we’ll move fast.
[19:10] Markus (Redwood): Okay.

[19:12] Priya (Northwind): One last question: does enabling v2 change cost?
[19:16] Markus (Redwood): Not directly. It may reduce latency which often reduces GPU time per request, so cost could improve. But pricing is based on the dedicated commit, not per request.
[19:28] Priya (Northwind): Right.

[19:30] Nina (Northwind): For hosted vs dedicated: if we decide dedicated, we still can keep the same API surface?
[19:35] Lauren (Redwood): Yes, same API, different endpoint and capacity guarantees.

[19:41] (pause)
[19:42] Markus (Redwood): Cool. We’ve got about 5 minutes—anything else on the tail latency explanation that we didn’t cover?
[19:49] Priya (Northwind): No, that was clear. The main takeaway is: start H100-only, keep deterministic, use allowlist, and monitor fallback rate.
[19:58] Omar (Redwood): Exactly.

[20:01] Markus (Redwood): Great. We’ll follow up via email with (1) the dedicated pool details, (2) the updated spreadsheet notes, and (3) the telemetry/query bundle. Thanks everyone.
[20:12] Priya (Northwind): Thanks.
[20:13] Nina (Northwind): Thank you.
[20:14] Tom (Northwind): Thanks all.

(Transcript continued with light scheduling / goodbye chatter)

[20:20] Lauren (Redwood): Priya, Tuesday morning or afternoon works better?
[20:23] Priya (Northwind): Afternoon.
[20:25] Markus (Redwood): Okay we’ll propose 2pm PT.
[20:28] Priya (Northwind): Sounds good.
[20:30] Omar (Redwood): I’ll get you the queries today.
[20:32] Priya (Northwind): Great.

End of recording
